whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the CRM Analytics Einstein Discovery Consultant exam for?

personas.label: Analysts building in CRM Analytics
personas.description: You already make dashboards and now need the data layer: recipes, dataflows, security predicates and how predictions get back into Salesforce.

personas.label: Admins asked to own analytics
personas.description: Reports and dashboards have hit their limit and CRM Analytics is the next step. This covers what that involves.

personas.label: Consultants on analytics projects
personas.description: You scope and deliver these builds and need to know where the real constraints are, particularly around row-level security.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the CRM Analytics Einstein Discovery Consultant Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: Moderate, with a hard edge in two places. Row-level security through predicates and sharing inheritance is where candidates lose most marks, and Einstein Discovery model quality, bias checking and deployment is the part people have least hands-on experience with. The dashboard and dataset questions are fair.
bullets: 60 questions in 105 minutes. Some questions show a predicate or a recipe step and ask what it does.
Security is the hard section. Security predicates, inherited sharing, and what each one can and cannot express.
Einstein Discovery is half the exam's name. Story creation, model metrics, bias, and writing predictions back to records.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Two things tell you whether you are ready. Can you write a security predicate for a requirement such as managers see their team's rows, and say when inherited sharing is the better answer? And can you look at a story's model and say whether it is good enough to deploy, and why? If either is shaky, that is where the marks are.

examFormat.heading: CRM Analytics Einstein Discovery Consultant Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Proctored online or at a test centre. The shape of it:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions are a requirement followed by four approaches, often with more than one that would work. The distinguishing factor is usually maintainability: a recipe over a dataflow, inherited sharing over a hand-written predicate, standard embedding over custom code.
bestWayToPass: Build a recipe, not just a dashboard. Load data, join it, aggregate it, output a dataset. The transformation questions become obvious once you have done this.
Practise security predicates until the syntax is automatic. They are the most commonly failed topic and they are learnable in an afternoon.
Create a story end to end. Pick a dataset, let Discovery build a model, read the metrics, then deploy the prediction to an object. Doing it once covers a surprising amount of ground.
Know when SAQL is actually needed. Most dashboard work does not require it, and the exam tests whether you know where the line is as much as it tests the syntax.

certificationCard.description: Covers the full CRM Analytics build: getting data in with dataflows and recipes, designing lenses and dashboards, row-level security, and using Einstein Discovery to create stories, evaluate models and write predictions back onto Salesforce records.

keyConcepts.h2: CRM Analytics & Einstein Discovery: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Datasets, Dataflows and Recipes
blocks.body: Everything in CRM Analytics queries a dataset, which is a columnar snapshot built on a schedule rather than a live view of Salesforce data. You get data in through two tools. Dataflows are the older JSON-defined approach, built from nodes such as sfdcDigest to pull an object, augment to join, flatten to resolve a role hierarchy, and sfdcRegister to output. Recipes are the newer visual tool, built on Data Prep, and they can do everything a dataflow can plus transformations that are painful in JSON: clustering, prediction, formula columns, appends and joins with a preview at every step. For new work, recipes are the expected answer, and the exam leans that way. Two dataflow nodes keep appearing in questions regardless: augment, because joining is so common, and flatten, because it is the only way to turn a hierarchy into something you can filter on.

blocks.heading: Lenses, Dashboards and Bindings
blocks.body: A lens is a single exploration of one dataset. A dashboard assembles widgets, and the thing that makes dashboards hard is bindings: the expressions that let one widget drive another. Selection bindings take what the user has clicked and feed it into another query. Results bindings take the output of one query and use it in another, which is how you build a widget whose values depend on a calculation elsewhere. Pages let you split a dashboard into views without building separate dashboards. The design guidance the exam rewards is unexciting and consistent: filter at the dataset or query level rather than fetching everything and hiding it, limit the number of queries per dashboard because each is a round trip, and use faceting so related widgets filter together by default.

blocks.heading: Einstein Discovery Stories and Models
blocks.body: A story is what Discovery produces when you point it at a dataset and name an outcome variable. It analyses the drivers of that outcome and produces insights in four flavours: what happened, why it happened, what will happen, and what to do about it. Behind the insights sits a model, and the exam expects you to be able to judge one. For a numeric outcome you look at R squared and mean absolute error; for a binary outcome you look at the confusion matrix and measures derived from it. The quality checks matter as much as the metrics. Discovery flags variables that leak the answer, such as a field that is only populated after the outcome is known, and it supports bias detection on sensitive variables so you can see whether the model treats groups differently. A model with strong metrics and a leaking variable is worse than useless, and questions test that you would reject it.

blocks.heading: Deploying Predictions Back to Salesforce
blocks.body: A model only earns its keep when it reaches the people doing the work. Discovery deploys a prediction definition against a Salesforce object, which puts a prediction, the top drivers behind it, and suggested improvements onto the record, visible through the Einstein Predictions component. Predictions can be scored in real time as a user edits a record, or written in bulk to existing records. They can also be consumed in Flow, which is how you act on a score automatically rather than leaving it on screen. The points that get examined are the mapping step, where the model's variables must be matched to fields on the target object, and the distinction between scoring on demand and writing scores back to the records in bulk.

blocks.heading: Row-Level Security
blocks.body: This is the section that decides results. A dataset is a flat snapshot and does not inherit Salesforce record access by default, so when a dataset is registered it is visible in full to anyone who can see it. There are two ways to restrict it. A security predicate is a filter expression stored on the dataset and applied to every query, written against dataset columns and user attributes, for example 'OwnerId' == "$User.Id". Predicates can express hierarchies by combining a flattened role column with the running user's role. The alternative is inherited sharing, where the dataset is configured to respect the sharing of the underlying Salesforce object, which is simpler to maintain and the right answer when the requirement is just mirror Salesforce sharing. Inherited sharing has limits on the number of records it can handle, which is exactly the trade-off questions probe: use inheritance for straightforward sharing on moderate volumes, write a predicate when the rule is custom or the volume is large.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the CRM Analytics and Einstein Discovery Consultant Exam
scenarioTips.intro: This exam rewards having built something. The dashboard questions are forgiving; the security and model-quality questions are not.

blocks.heading: Recipes Over Dataflows
blocks.body: Recipes are the current tool and the expected answer for new work. Know what they add: formula columns, clustering, prediction, visual previews.

blocks.heading: Predicate Syntax
blocks.body: Practise writing predicates for real requirements, including owner-based and role-hierarchy cases. The most commonly failed topic and the most quickly fixed.

blocks.heading: Inherited Sharing Trade-off
blocks.body: Simpler to maintain, limited by record volume. Know when to choose it over a predicate and be ready to justify either.

blocks.heading: Judging a Model
blocks.body: R squared and mean absolute error for numeric outcomes, the confusion matrix for binary ones. Watch for leaking variables and check bias on sensitive fields.

blocks.heading: Bindings
blocks.body: Selection bindings respond to clicks; results bindings use one query's output in another. Build one of each rather than reading about them.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Consultant Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: Where analytics work usually leads next:

sampleQuestions.question: A dataset must show each user only the records they own. Which approach expresses this most directly?
options: Removing the dataset from all apps
A security predicate comparing the owner column to the running user's ID
Field-level security on the source object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Security predicates are applied to every query against the dataset and are designed for exactly this rule.
whyWrong: A dashboard filter can be removed by the user and is not a security control.
Hiding the dataset blocks legitimate access rather than filtering rows.
Field-level security on the source object does not restrict rows in a registered dataset.

sampleQuestions.question: A requirement is simply that the dataset should respect the sharing already configured on the Salesforce object, and record volume is moderate. What is the best choice?
options: No restriction, relying on app permissions
A hand-written security predicate replicating the sharing rules
sampleQuestions.explanation: Inherited sharing mirrors Salesforce sharing without you maintaining a parallel rule set, which is why it suits this case.
whyWrong: App-level permissions control who sees the dataset, not which rows.
Duplicating datasets per role multiplies maintenance and refresh cost.
Replicating sharing in a predicate is more work to build and to keep correct.

sampleQuestions.question: An Einstein Discovery model shows excellent accuracy, but one of its variables is only populated after the outcome has been decided. What should happen?
options: Deploy it, since the accuracy is high
Convert it to a text field
Keep it but document the issue
sampleQuestions.explanation: A variable known only after the outcome inflates accuracy in training and is useless at prediction time.
whyWrong: High accuracy caused by leakage will not survive contact with real data.
Changing the field type does not change when the value becomes known.
Documenting a broken model does not make it safe to deploy.

sampleQuestions.question: Which dataflow node joins columns from one dataset onto another?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Augment is the join node, bringing fields from a right dataset onto a left one on a matching key.
whyWrong: sfdcDigest extracts data from a Salesforce object.
sfdcRegister writes the result out as a dataset.
Flatten resolves a hierarchy into a column of ancestor values.

sampleQuestions.question: A dashboard must show a chart whose values depend on the result of a separate query rather than on a user click. What is needed?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Results bindings feed the output of one query into another, independent of user interaction.
whyWrong: Predicates are a security mechanism.
A new dataset does not create the dependency between widgets.
Selection bindings respond to what the user has clicked.

sampleQuestions.question: For new data preparation work in CRM Analytics, which tool is the expected choice?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Recipes are the current tool and cover everything dataflows do plus transformations that are difficult in JSON.
whyWrong: Report snapshots are a core Salesforce feature, unrelated to CRM Analytics datasets.
Apex is not how CRM Analytics datasets are built.
Dataflows remain supported but are no longer the recommended starting point.

sampleQuestions.question: A deployed prediction should trigger an automated follow-up task when the score falls below a threshold. How is this best done?
options: Ask users to read the score and act manually
Add a formula field on the dashboard
Consume the prediction in Flow and create the task there
Rebuild the model with a lower threshold
sampleQuestions.explanation: Predictions can be consumed in Flow, which is how a score drives automated action.
whyWrong: Manual action does not satisfy an automation requirement.
Dashboards display information and cannot create records.
Changing the model does not create the follow-up task.

sampleQuestions.question: Which dataflow node is required to filter on a role hierarchy within a dataset?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Flatten converts a hierarchy into a multi-value column of ancestors, which a predicate or filter can then use.
whyWrong: Augment joins datasets but does not resolve hierarchy paths.
dim2mea converts a dimension to a measure.
Slice selects or removes fields.

sampleQuestions.question: Which metrics are appropriate for judging a model that predicts a numeric outcome such as deal amount?
options: R squared and mean absolute error
sampleQuestions.explanation: Numeric outcomes are evaluated with regression measures such as R squared and mean absolute error.
whyWrong: Precision and recall are classification measures.
Confusion matrices describe classification outcomes.
Insight count says nothing about model quality.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does a CRM Analytics dashboard get slower as more widgets are added?
options: Widgets are rendered sequentially on the server
Each query is a separate round trip against the dataset
Security predicates are re-evaluated per user session only
sampleQuestions.explanation: Query count is the main driver of dashboard performance, which is why consolidating and faceting helps.
whyWrong: Rendering is not the bottleneck; querying is.
Datasets are fixed snapshots and do not grow when widgets are added.
Predicate evaluation is not the cause of the scaling problem described.

sampleQuestions.question: A sensitive variable such as gender is present in a story's dataset. What should be done before deploying?
options: Ignore it, since models are objective
Run bias detection to see whether outcomes differ by group
sampleQuestions.explanation: Discovery supports bias checking on sensitive variables, and checking is the responsible step before deployment.
whyWrong: Models reproduce patterns in their training data, including unfair ones.
Deleting the dataset discards work that may be legitimate once checked.
Changing the field type does not address the fairness question.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the relationship between a dataset and live Salesforce data?
options: A dataset is a report type
A dataset is a snapshot refreshed on a schedule
A dataset queries Salesforce records in real time
A dataset is a view over the Salesforce database
sampleQuestions.explanation: Datasets are built and refreshed by dataflows or recipes, so they reflect data as of the last run.
whyWrong: Report types are a core reporting concept.
Real-time querying is not how CRM Analytics datasets work.
There is no live view; the data is copied in.

sampleQuestions.question: A prediction definition is being deployed to the Opportunity object. Which step is essential?
options: Mapping the model's variables to fields on the object
Writing a security predicate for the model
sampleQuestions.explanation: Variable to field mapping is what lets the model score live records on the target object.
whyWrong: Bindings are a dashboard construct.
Predicates secure dataset rows and are not part of prediction mapping.
A dataflow is not required to deploy an existing model.

sampleQuestions.question: When is writing SAQL by hand the appropriate choice?
options: When a query cannot be expressed through the standard dashboard query builder
sampleQuestions.explanation: Most dashboard work needs no SAQL, so hand-written queries are for the cases the builder cannot express.
whyWrong: Routine widgets are better built with the standard tooling and are easier to maintain.
SAQL queries data; recipes prepare it.
Hand-written SAQL is not automatically faster.

sampleQuestions.question: A manager must see rows belonging to everyone beneath them in the role hierarchy. Which combination achieves this?
options: Field-level security on the role field
A dashboard filter on manager name
A flattened role column plus a predicate referencing the running user's role
sampleQuestions.explanation: Flattening produces the ancestor path, and the predicate then compares it against the running user.
whyWrong: Field-level security does not filter rows.
Dashboard filters are not a security control.
Building a dashboard per manager does not scale and leaves the data unsecured.
